title: Pit three olives with a plier pitter: olive upright in the cup, squeezed through, stone to a ramekin, olive to a bowl
instruction: Pit the three olives with the pitter: the pitted olives go in the bowl and the stones in the ramekin.
context: Pitting olives or cherries with a hand pitter is a common kitchen job at home and in restaurant prep. The plier-style pitter (like the OXO Good Grips Cherry & Olive Pitter) is used as its retailers describe: the fruit goes in the front chamber, the handle is squeezed, and the stone drops out through the splatter shield. The hand skill: the pitter lies on the table and must be picked up by its handles and turned cup up in the hand, held only by squeezing its handles against their spring; each slick 22 x 18 mm olive is picked up, turned end up and set into a 19.6 mm cup under the raised plunger, centred to 3 mm and upright to 25 deg (otherwise the plunger tears its side and the stone stays in); the handles are squeezed fully shut against the spring (about 20-30 N); and the pitted olive is tipped out over the bowl. One hand holds and works the pitter while the other loads the olives.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Plier-style cherry and olive pitter (like the OXO Good Grips Cherry & Olive Pitter), 14.6 cm long, 100 g, die-cast handles 2.8 cm wide hinged at one end, held 30 deg open by its spring; the cup ring (2.8 cm across, 19.6 mm bore over a 12 mm hole) at the other end of the lower handle, the plunger on the upper handle over it. Loose, lying on its side (hinge axis vertical): hinge at x 12, y -20, the cup end toward +y at y -7.5, the upper handle on the far side (+x). (2) White saucer 14 cm across, 4 mm thick, at x 20, y 14, loose. (3) Three large green olives with stones (for example Manzanilla), about 22 x 18 mm and 7 g, drained, lying on the saucer along y at x 16, 20 and 24, y 14. (4) White ceramic ramekin for the stones, 9 cm across inside, 3.5 cm deep, 250 g, at x 28, y 0, loose. (5) Bowl for the pitted olives, 9.6 cm across inside, 4.5 cm deep, 300 g, at x 16.5, y 0, loose. Both arms start at the ready pose, grippers open. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Every control step: the handles' angle, each olive's and stone's pose and each finger's collision points. When the handles are squeezed to within 1.5 deg of shut, an olive in the cup is pitted if its centre is within 3 mm of the cup's axis and 4 mm of the seated height and its long axis within 25 deg of the plunger (its stone is then let go); otherwise it is torn and keeps its stone. Per olive, 1/6 each: its stone lies in the ramekin; it was pitted (not torn) and lies in the bowl, released (every finger point 1 cm or more away) and still. Score = sum; 1.0 (success, held 1 s) = all six. Real trial: count the stones in the ramekin and check each olive in the bowl: a hole through its ends, no split side.
reset_notes: Replace the three olives with new ones from the jar, drained and patted dry, laid on the saucer as in the screenshot; empty and wipe the ramekin and the bowl; rinse and dry the pitter and lay it on its side, handles open, as in the screenshot. Simulation: each trial starts the simulator afresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at true size; the olive is a rigid capsule with its stone a separate body fixed inside, and the flesh is not cut. The plunger and the upper handle's front arm pass through the olive: at full stroke (1.9 N m against the spring, 20-30 N across the handles) a seated, centred, upright olive has its stone let go to fall through the cup's hole; otherwise it counts as torn. A wet olive's friction is 0.25. The splatter shield is drawn only.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right gripper hovered over the lying pitter and never picked it up; the left hovered over the saucer and later knocked the olives off it; no olive reached the cup); demo: 1.0
